name: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: 2012 International TSC Consensus Conference Diagnostic Criteria (Updated 2021)

criteria.description: Facial angiofibromas (>= 3) or fibrous cephalic plaque
Cortical dysplasias (including tubers and cerebral white matter radial migration lines)
Pathogenic variant in TSC1 or TSC2

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Definite TSC: 2 major features, or 1 major + 2 minor features, or pathogenic TSC1/TSC2 mutation. Possible TSC: 1 major feature, or 2 or more minor features.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: LAM alone is insufficient for definite diagnosis without other features. Cardiac rhabdomyomas are often the first finding (prenatal ultrasound). Two-thirds of cases are de novo.

pathognomonic.notes: Red-pink papules in butterfly distribution on face; typically appear by age 3-5 years
Areas of cortical dysplasia seen on MRI; hallmark brain lesion

common.notes: Often first clinical sign; best seen with Wood lamp
Infantile spasms in ~35% of infants; multiple seizure types common
Ranges from normal intelligence to severe ID; correlates with seizure burden
Often detected prenatally; spontaneous regression common in childhood

occasional.notes: Can cause obstructive hydrocephalus; requires surveillance
Orange-peel textured plaque, typically on lower back
Flesh-colored growths around fingernails/toenails; appear after puberty

rare.notes: Progressive cystic lung disease; predominantly affects adult women
Risk increases with AML size >4 cm

laboratory: Renal function tests for monitoring kidney involvement
VEGF-D levels (biomarker for LAM in women)
imaging: Brain MRI: cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, white matter radial migration lines, SEGA
Renal MRI or ultrasound: angiomyolipomas, renal cysts
Chest CT (HRCT): LAM in adult women
Abdominal MRI preferred over CT for lifelong renal surveillance (radiation avoidance)
genetic: TSC1 gene mutations (hamartin, chromosome 9q34) ~30% of identified mutations
TSC2 gene mutations (tuberin, chromosome 16p13) ~70% of identified mutations
TSC2 mutations tend to cause more severe disease
~65-75% of cases are de novo; ~25-35% inherited (autosomal dominant)
~10-25% of clinically definite TSC have no identifiable mutation (mosaicism suspected)
other: Wood lamp examination for hypomelanotic macules
Dental examination for enamel pits and gingival fibromas

distinguishingFeatures: NF1 has cafe-au-lait macules (hyperpigmented, not hypopigmented)
NF1 has neurofibromas rather than angiofibromas
Isolated cortical malformation without systemic features
Renal tumors (chromophobe, oncocytic) rather than AML

redFlags: Growing SEGA with risk of obstructive hydrocephalus (neurosurgical emergency)
Large renal AML (>4 cm) with hemorrhage risk
Cardiac rhabdomyoma causing arrhythmia or outflow obstruction in neonates
references: Northrup H, et al. Tuberous sclerosis complex diagnostic criteria update: recommendations of the 2012 International Tuberous Sclerosis Complex Consensus Conference. Pediatr Neurol. 2013;49(4):243-254.

Krueger DA, et al. Tuberous sclerosis complex surveillance and management: recommendations of the 2012 International Tuberous Sclerosis Complex Consensus Conference. Pediatr Neurol. 2013;49(4):255-265.
Curatolo P, et al. Tuberous sclerosis. Lancet. 2008;372(9639):657-668.
Henske EP, et al. Tuberous sclerosis complex. Nat Rev Dis Primers. 2016;2:16035.
